speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Two relate to the introduction of measures to enhance the Comptroller of GST’s powers to safeguard public monies and investigate tax offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The other five arise from our periodic review of the GST regime to clarify technical rules and improve on administration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MOF sought views from the public on the draft Bill earlier this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have evaluated the feedback received and incorporated them where they are relevant to the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, we introduce three measures to counter Missing Trader Fraud.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other jurisdictions and in Singapore too, there have been multiple attempts to use Missing Trader Fraud to defraud the tax authorities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, in the European Union, Missing Trader Fraud has cost around 60 billion Euros annually.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Disrupting the capacity of organised crime groups involved in Missing Trader Fraud is one of the EU’s priority crime areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Basically, all GST-registered businesses are required to charge GST when they sell goods or services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These businesses are supposed to pay the output GST to IRAS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: GST-registered businesses who incur GST on their purchases of goods and services may claim a refund of this GST from IRAS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Missing Trader Fraud is a fraud scheme used by syndicates, where a party who has collected output GST and is supposed to pay it to IRAS absconds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This party is, therefore, known as the Missing Trader.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Meanwhile, parties downstream of the chain continue to make input GST claims to IRAS, on purchases that they had made.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Syndicates make the detection of Missing Trader Fraud difficult, by interposing many businesses along the chain to deter IRAS from tracing back to the Missing Trader.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, businesses which IRAS have found to be involved in Missing Trader Fraud will have their input GST claims denied, as they have not fulfilled the conditions for claiming input GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The purchases that such businesses made and are seeking input GST claims on were not genuine business transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Beyond this, it is also important that we stop Missing Trader Fraud from being attempted across the value chain in the first instance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is critical that all GST-registered businesses undertake adequate and appropriate due diligence checks, as well as precautions, to avoid being in a fraudulent arrangement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Doing so is also in the interest of all businesses, as part of good corporate governance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Bona fide businesses generally already conduct due diligence checks on their transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The first set of amendments will allow us to put in place three measures to deter Missing Trader Fraud.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The burden of proving that the business knew or should have known of the fraudulent arrangement lies on the Comptroller, with the standard of proof being the balance of probabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And I should note that this measure is similar to the approach taken in the United Kingdom and the EU to safeguard tax revenue.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Again, this surcharge serves as a deterrent effect and we will review the surcharge quantum periodically.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Other jurisdictions do likewise with a surcharge to serve as a deterrence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It also allows the Comptroller to deny a GST registration, or cancel GST registration if any of the conditions imposed is breached.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The three measures under the first amendment can be found in clauses 4, 6, 7, 10 to 13, 20 and 22 of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The second amendment enhances IRAS’s powers to seize goods for investigation of tax offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This amendment empowers specially authorised IRAS officers to seize or prohibit the disposal of or dealing in, any goods suspected or intended to be used to commit an offence under the GST Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The seizure powers also include goods which may aid in the investigation or prosecution of such an offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This prevents syndicates from using the goods to perpetuate fraud, and it is an important measure in disrupting the operations of fraud schemes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 2, 5, 13, 14 to 17 and 25 in the Bill provide for this change.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Beyond these two sets of amendments, MOF regularly reviews the GST regime to clarify technical rules and to improve GST administration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The first two amendments arising from this periodic review relate to enhancing our GST rules to counteract tax avoidance arrangements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This seeks to maintain a certain level of consistency across the Comptroller's treatment of GST tax avoidance arrangements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The amendment also expands the tax avoidance rules to include GST avoidance arrangements that result in an earlier entitlement to input tax claims or to unjustified bad debt relief claims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Under the amendment, tax adjustments by the Comptroller to counteract tax avoidance arrangements must be made within five years from the end of the relevant GST accounting period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The taxpayer will also be required to pay the additional GST arising from the Comptroller’s tax adjustments within one month.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These changes to our GST rules to counteract tax avoidance arrangements are found in clauses 8 and 12 of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is similar to what we had just discussed and passed earlier in the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, there is no such surcharge – instead, the Comptroller’s adjustments under the anti-avoidance rules only restore taxpayers to their initial tax position, as if the arrangement had not been entered into.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is insufficient to deter aggressive taxpayers from taking the risk of later adjustments made by the Comptroller to counteract the tax avoidance arrangement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 9 and 12 in the Bill provides for these changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The third amendment arising from our periodic review seeks to provide certainty to taxpayers, by clarifying the treatment of claims relating to overpaid or erroneously paid GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For instance, the GST Act currently allows a person to claim a refund of money that has been overpaid or paid erroneously as GST, such as GST that was wrongly charged on non-taxable transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These changes are found in clause 19 in the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The fourth set of amendments seek to encourage taxpayers to benefit from the convenience of digital services and allow them to get refunds faster.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And just as I mentioned for the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill, in this case an assessment of the readiness of GST-registered businesses will be made next year, and exceptions will be provided where necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 18 of the Bill provides for this amendment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This amendment is found in clauses 3, 21 and 24 in the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A similar amendment was proposed for the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill just now.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Particularly against this backdrop, I agree in principle that strengthening measures to enhance the Comptroller of GST's powers to safeguard public monies and minimise the loss of public revenues is of utmost importance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The introduction of measures to counter Missing Trader Fraud and counteract tax avoidance arrangement in the GST (Amendment) Bill is thus timely.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the EU, it is estimated that the losses from VAT fraud amounts to 60 billion Euros annually, as Second Minister Lawrence Wong has mentioned in his speech.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In addition, I am also concerned about the potential impact of the amendments to SMEs who are already facing resource constraints.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Section 20, subsection (2)(d) to (f) specify the conditions to reach a taxable person should have known that the supply made to the taxable person was part of an arrangement to cause loss of public revenues.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These include whether the circumstances are such that there was a reasonable risk of the supply being part of the fraudulent arrangement and, hence, whether or not taxable person took reasonable steps to ascertain these.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, even if the taxable person had taken reasonable steps and arrived at the wrong conclusion, it does not spare the taxable person from being taken that he should have known that the arrangement was fraudulent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would this be potentially onerous on companies, especially SMEs who may not have the same capabilities to conduct extensive due diligence, as compared to larger companies with greater economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Codification of what the reasonable person or reasonable steps mean would thus be critical for SMEs to not fall foul of new requirements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet while we are looking to address the loss of public revenues via Missing Trader Fraud with this amendment, I would also like to take the opportunity to ask the Ministry what has been the progress of the Government's study on an e-commerce tax?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Budget 2018, I note the Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat's announcement that the Government will introduce GST on imported services with effect from 1 January 2020 or what we commonly call a “Netflix tax”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is to make sure that our tax system remains fair and resilient in the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For the import of goods, I noted Minister Heng Swee Keat then remarks and, I quote, "For the import of goods, there are international discussions on how GST can apply.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We will review this before deciding on the measure to take." The OECD has since endorsed new rules and frameworks for the collection of taxes on online sale of goods in March 2019.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As we look to support SME retailers with the Rental Relief Framework while providing support to employment via the JSS, it is perhaps now timely to look into addressing a growing source of tax leakage due to overseas online retailers and correct the key imbalance faced by tax-paying retailers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More broadly, the liquidation of Robinson's after more than 162 years of operation here in Singapore is perhaps a grim reminder of the state of the retail landscape in Singapore today and how more needs to be done to address the various costs of doing business.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But the changing economic and retail landscape is perhaps a timely reminder of our need to continue addressing other forms of GST leakage and exploring other forms of revenue sources before looking to an eventual GST hike to raise tax revenues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is more crucial now than ever in the existing financial climate to ensure that tax revenue is protected from fraud or loopholes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I have four points of clarification on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, I would like to clarify how we are supporting SMEs’ compliance with due diligence requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the need for businesses to step up and take reasonable steps against fraud.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, big businesses and small businesses have different resources and capacity to conduct checks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is a reasonable step for a big business and a small business may not be the same.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister clarify how it will ensure that such requirements do not constitute an onerous burden to our SMEs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am aware that the Minister plans to provide guidance for businesses on what constitutes “reasonable steps” in section 20.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond that, can the Ministry share whether it will offer training and industry-specific resources to ensure small businesses can still effectively conduct their due diligence checks?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point of clarification is on the Comptroller’s review process when investigating fraudulent arrangements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A company involved in fraudulent arrangements could face the severe penalty of deregistration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the key considerations the Comptroller will take into account when evaluating a company’s involvement in fraud?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, in the UK, adequate and timely checks by the company to ensure the integrity of its supply chain will be viewed favourably.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Providing these key considerations will be useful in guiding honest businesses in their due diligence checks so as to mitigate risks of an unwitting involvement in fraud.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Because the level of checks expected for business sectors that are commercially risky or vulnerable to fraud and other criminality is higher, can I propose that the Minister identifies these sectors so businesses know to step up their due diligence checks and also share a separate set of key considerations businesses in these sectors can align to?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that we also expect more intensive checks for industries more susceptible to fraud and criminal activities, can the Minister identify such industries and share additional guidelines specific to these industries?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, if we are going to ask more of certain businesses, it will help if we can also provide more support for their compliance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can I also request the Minister to then share and incorporate these guidelines in the IRAS e-Tax Guide so businesses are able to access this information easily?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point of clarification is on the documentation businesses are expected to maintain as part of their due diligence checks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify in regulations or codes the methods and level of detail of documentation businesses are expected to maintain to be deemed to have taken “reasonable steps to ascertain whether the supply was part of a fraudulent arrangement”?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify for how long businesses are expected to retain these documentations, given that the timeframe for the Comptroller to determine if a supply is part of a Missing Trader Fraud is open-ended?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We want to avoid the situation where honest businesses do their due diligence checks but cannot back it up because they discarded or deleted supporting documents after a period of time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We also want to avoid the situation where fraudulent businesses can realistically claim to have discarded supporting documents even when no such checks were done.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point is a proposal for an anonymous reporting channel for whistleblowers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Businesses or individuals may, in the course of their due diligence checks, come across potentially fraudulent suppliers or entities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must make sure businesses or individuals feel safe coming forward.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, it is unclear the parties who will be privy to the tip beyond the generic email provided at ifd@iras.gov.sg on IRAS' “Report Tax Evasion” website.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And if these parties are the very target of the tip, there should be an alternate reporting channel whistleblowers can turn to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the parties that are privy to the tips sent to the IRAS email address mentioned and whether there are alternate reporting channels for whistleblowers to report suspicious or fraudulent arrangements that are potentially related to these very officers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister confirm that this information will be reflected on IRAS’ “Report Tax Evasion” website so whistleblowers are aware of their options?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Chua asked about the extent of missing trader fraud in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not at the same scale as the EU, but we see the trends internationally.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are concerned and that is why we are putting in place these measures and I am very happy that Mr Louis Chua also supports them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, Mr Louis Chua also mentioned the possibility of doing an e-commerce tax and I am very happy that he supports this, too, because we will certainly look for ways to raise more revenues.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have already moved on GST for imported services and we will be looking at the GST for imported goods, too.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is something that is quite complex because the way to go about doing this, obviously, is to tax at source, right?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When you buy something from an e-commerce platform, impose the GST at source and then you can ensure that GST applies even for e-commerce transactions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if countries do not all impose such a tax, it is quite easy to circumvent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You can imagine shipments being sent to different countries in order to bypass.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there are some complexities around this but we are studying this very carefully with a view towards putting in place a proper regime to ensure that the e-commerce transactions are also subject to GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will be updating the House in due course when we are ready with this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, Mr Louis Chua and Mr Louis Ng both highlighted concerns about the compliance burden that would be imposed on SMEs and we are equally concerned.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let me share some of the ways in which we are intending to deal with this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With regard to, for example, guidance to SMEs on the due diligence checks that they have to make, how can we provide more clarity?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Today, IRAS already provides and makes available such guidance, and it will continue to educate taxpayers on the kinds of due diligence checks that are necessary.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Besides providing ready information on its website and through the media, IRAS has been engaging industry associations and tax intermediaries to raise industry awareness.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Newly GST-registered businesses can also access e-learning and other resources on IRAS' website, so that all these will help them to understand and better comply with the GST obligations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As is the case with previous legislative updates, IRAS will publish an e-tax guide soon after the Bill comes into force and this will provide businesses with the latest guidance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The e-tax guide will highlight examples of risk indicators that a business ought to take notice of in relation to a supply that might be part of a missing trader fraud arrangement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, hopefully, SMEs will start to be more aware of what they should be looking out for and we will also provide some illustrations of the due diligence checks that businesses should take in response to the risk identified.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And the Comptroller of GST will take into account all the facts and circumstances of each case, including the firm's circumstances as an SME, where relevant, in considering what is reasonable.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS will also work with interested industry associations to conduct dedicated outreach sessions and businesses may contact IRAS if they require further information.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Ng sought clarification on how the Comptroller of GST will assess whether a GST-registered business knew or should have known that its purchase was part of a fraudulent arrangement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Comptroller's assessment depends on the facts and circumstances of each case and will include taking into account all the relevant considerations, like whether due diligence and risk assessment checks were performed by the business, what were the results of these checks, to what extent were the checks appropriate, adequate and timely to address the risks identified and whether the taxable person took appropriate action in response to the results of these checks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And businesses that disagree with the Comptroller's decision may apply for review and revision of the decision under section 49 of the GST Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if businesses disagree with the Comptroller's review and revision of the decision, they then may appeal further to the GST Board of Review.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, again, if they are dissatisfied with the decision of the Board, they can appeal to the High Court.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Ng asked for the level of detail and duration that GST-registered businesses must maintain the documents or the records of reasonable steps that they have taken to determine whether a supply made to them was part of a fraudulent arrangement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, on record-keeping of documents, what constitutes reasonable steps?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As advised on IRAS' website, businesses today must already keep proper records and accounts of business transactions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This includes retaining the source documents, accounting records and schedules, bank statements and any other records of transactions connected with the business.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This information should be made available upon request by IRAS to ensure there is proper accountability for decisions made.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Again, IRAS will make all this information available in its e-tax guide.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As Mr Ng highlighted, IRAS' Investigation and Forensics Division maintains a mailbox that businesses or individuals may utilise to notify IRAS of any possible case of tax evasion or tax avoidance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This information including examples of signs of tax evasion and information that may be useful to IRAS is published on IRAS's website.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Alternatively, if the whistleblower suspects that an IRAS officer is involved in a corrupt act, the whistleblower may lodge a complaint with the CPIB.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is critical that all GST-registered businesses undertake adequate and appropriate due diligence checks as well as precautions to avoid being involved in a fraudulent arrangement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are critical steps that we will need to safeguard and preserve our revenue base.
